target.title: EMG-to-Speech: Direct Generation of Speech from Facial Electromyographic Signals
target.venue: IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing 25(12):2375-2385

entries.text: The authors state that the work establishes a label-free approach, contrasting it with recognition-followed-by-synthesis.
entries.quote: this work establishes a label-free approach

entries.text: The LDA projection is computed from phone sub-state labels force-aligned using the simultaneously recorded audio.
The LDA output is truncated to 32 dimensions.
entries.quote: truncated to the 32 highest-discriminability dimensions

entries.text: Two input sets are used: high-dimensional TD15 features and the LDA-reduced 32-dimensional features (GMM and one LSTM variant use LDA input, Table II).
entries.quote: reduced to 32 dimensions using LDA

entries.text: All EMG in the paper is recorded during audible speech.
entries.quote: In this paper we use EMG recorded during audible speech and perform a direct conversion to speech.

entries.text: The authors state that a truly silent system is possible but is not what the paper tests.
The corpus table is titled as audible EMG data only.
Six sessions from three speakers.
Corpus totals: 4,552 training, 504 development and 83 evaluation utterances (05:39 min of evaluation audio).
Per-session evaluation sets hold 10 to 20 utterances; e.g. S1-Array-Lrg has 984 training and 10 evaluation utterances.
Mean evaluation MCD: DNN 5.21, significantly best (p < 0.01).
entries.quote: DNNs give the best results by a significant margin (p < 0.01) with a mean MCD of 5.21

entries.text: Mean MCD LSTM 5.46 vs Unit Selection 5.42.
entries.quote: between LSTM and Unit Selection (mean MCD of 5.46 vs 5.42)

entries.text: Gaussian Mapping mean MCD 5.69 (worst).
entries.quote: Gaussian Mapping obtains the highest (worst) average MCD with 5.69

entries.text: Best session-dependent MCD 4.56 on Spk1-Array-Large.
entries.quote: session-dependent result is achieved on the Spk1-Array-Large

entries.text: The text states the best performance is improved to 4.51, a value not shown in the evaluation results (best evaluation session 4.56).
entries.quote: our current results improve the best performance to 4.51

entries.text: The comparison baseline is Toth et al. at MCD 6.37.
entries.quote: introduced an MCD of 6.37

entries.text: Single-electrode versus array setups show no clear MCD tendency.
The ASR used for intelligibility is trained on synthesized output of the EMG training set.
entries.quote: output that was generated from the EMG training set input

entries.text: The ASR uses a trigram language model.
entries.quote: a trigram language model

entries.text: ASR evaluation uses three decoding vocabularies (108, 905, 2,111 words) and only two speakers.
entries.quote: 108, 905 and 2,111 words, evaluated for two different speakers

entries.text: Mean WER 7.3% at 108 words vs 10.9% for the EMG-ASR of Wand et al. with 160 training utterances.
entries.quote: achieve an average WER of 10.9 % using a vocabulary of 108 words with 160 training utterances, while we report a mean WER of 7.3 % using our synthesized speech approach
entries.condition: 108-word vocabulary, trigram LM; training sizes differ

entries.text: The authors concede the WER comparison is not direct.
entries.quote: While a direct comparison is difficult, we have shown that good performance can be achieved when the synthesized output is used on an ASR system.

entries.text: The authors argue a GMM bias in the ASR evaluation is unlikely.
The naturalness test uses reference MFCCs and varies only the excitation; called a preliminary experiment.
entries.quote: we conduct a preliminary experiment: We use the target

entries.text: Naturalness stimuli: three utterances from each of four speakers (12 utterances), although the corpus has three speakers.
Naturalness test with 20 participants.
Naturalness scores: reference 81, resynthesized 41, EMG-to-F0 28, zero F0 22, flat F0 7.
EMG-to-F0 is significantly more natural than the two artificial F0 schemes.
entries.quote: significantly (p < 0.01) gives the most natural output among the three F0 generation methods

entries.text: DNN output preferred in more than 50% of cases; Unit Selection never preferred.
Run time is pure feature-mapping time; vocoding and file I/O are omitted.
Run time is measured on the whole evaluation set as one batch.
DNN mapping is faster than 0.1x real time and called the preferred choice for an online system.
The LSTMs are bidirectional.
entries.quote: The LSTMs used in this work are bidirectional LSTMs

entries.text: Unit Selection stays above real time even with clustering.
Faulty channels are removed by manual inspection per session.
Parameters were tuned on a development set.
Conclusion: no restriction to a phone set, vocabulary or language.
Conclusion: paralinguistic cues and voice characteristics can be preserved because direct mapping models them implicitly.
Conclusion: the DNN performs best in real-time behaviour, naturalness and intelligibility.
MLSA vocoding is described as simple; other schemes gave no significant gain.

No random seeds, repeated training runs or confidence intervals are reported for MCD, WER or listener results; error bars are standard deviations over utterances.
entries.quote: Error bars show standard deviation.

entries.text: The statistical test behind the p < 0.01 claims is not named.
Every model is trained and tested within one session (session-dependent); no cross-session or cross-speaker test is reported.
The paper does not state whether the LDA matrix is estimated on training data only.
The naturalness test does not say which mapping method produced the EMG-to-F0 contour, and no mapping-method comparison of naturalness is reported.
No silent-articulation (mouthed) test data are used anywhere in the article.
Toth 2009: GMM EMG-to-speech, 64 components, mean MCD 6.37 (std 2.34).

questions.q: Which text does the wiki folder hold, and what was the previous notes.json built from?
questions.answer: The wiki folder holds the 2016 KIT dissertation (manifest version kit-dissertation-2016); the previous notes were built from it and are kept as notes.dissertation.json. These notes are rebuilt from the TASLP article text.

questions.q: Does the article test silent EMG?
questions.answer: No. All data are audible EMG (Table I); the silent-EMG experiments exist only in the dissertation.

questions.q: Which Fig. 5 values belong to the single-electrode sessions?
questions.answer: Read from the PDF figure (page 7): x-axis order Spk1-Array-Large, Spk1-Array, Spk2-Single, Spk2-Array, Spk3-Array-Large, Spk1-Single; DNN 4.56, 4.94, 5.29, 5.44, 5.44, 5.61.
